candidate_lines.L002: This 39-week neonate presents with critical early-onset sepsis, evidenced by culture-confirmed bacteremia, severe respiratory distress requiring CPAP, and signs of shock (poor perfusion, lethargy). The clinical picture is driven by significant maternal risk factors including chorioamnionitis, GBS colonization without adequate intrapartum prophylaxis, and prolonged rupture of membranes.
candidate_lines.L005: The patient is classified as CRITICAL risk (Score 14) due to the presence of culture-confirmed bacteremia (Layer 3, 4 points), clinical chorioamnionitis (Layer 1, 3 points), and severe physiological compromise including respiratory distress and poor perfusion. The combination of maternal GBS positivity without adequate intrapartum antibiotics and prolonged ROM further elevates the probability of severe infection to 45.0 per 1000.
candidate_lines.L008: Maternal GBS colonization without adequate IAP contributes 2 points (Layer 1). Prolonged ROM (40h) contributes 2 points (Layer 1). Maternal intrapartum fever (39.1C) contributes 2 points (Layer 1). Clinical chorioamnionitis contributes 3 points (Layer 1). Severe respiratory distress contributes 2 points (Layer 2). Elevated CRP (65.0 mg/L) contributes 2 points (Layer 3). Positive blood culture contributes 4 points (Layer 3). Poor perfusion/shock signs contribute 2 points (Layer 2).
candidate_lines.L011: - Initiate immediate empiric antibiotic therapy with IV ampicillin and IV gentamicin as per WHO guidelines for critical illness.
candidate_lines.L012: - Provide respiratory support with CPAP and monitor oxygen saturation closely.
candidate_lines.L013: - Manage hemodynamic instability with fluid resuscitation and vasopressors if indicated by poor perfusion.
candidate_lines.L014: - Obtain repeat blood cultures to monitor clearance of bacteremia.
candidate_lines.L015: - Monitor for signs of meningitis given the severity of illness and positive blood culture.
candidate_lines.L018: - IV ampicillin — Dose and frequency not specified in retrieved WHO guideline excerpts; consult local hospital protocol or full WHO guideline for specific mg/kg dosing.
candidate_lines.L019: - IV gentamicin — Dose and frequency not specified in retrieved WHO guideline excerpts; consult local hospital protocol or full WHO guideline for specific mg/kg dosing.
candidate_lines.L020: duration=At least 10 days stop_criteria=Clinical improvement, negative follow-up blood cultures, and resolution of inflammatory markers (CRP/PCT) as per clinical judgment and full guideline recommendations.
candidate_lines.L023: Continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring. Monitor temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, and oxygen saturation every 1-2 hours. Assess perfusion (capillary refill time, skin color) and neurological status (lethargy, tone) every 4 hours. Monitor urine output hourly. Repeat CRP and PCT every 24-48 hours. Monitor renal function (creatinine) and electrolytes daily.
candidate_lines.L026: Worsening respiratory distress requiring intubation, persistent or worsening shock despite fluid resuscitation, new onset seizures, or failure to clear bacteremia after 48-72 hours of appropriate antibiotic therapy.
candidate_lines.L029: Initiate intravenous fluids for hydration and maintenance, adjusting for insensible losses and shock state. Consider trophic feeds if hemodynamically stable, otherwise maintain NPO status until perfusion improves. Monitor fluid balance strictly.

passage_catalog.S002:
Source: WHO
Section: Recommendation A.2 (UPDATED)
Recommendation: rec1

Recommendation: Young infants aged 0–59 days with the IMCI signs of critical illness should be referred to hospital. If referral is not possible, ampicillin IM/IV plus gentamicin IM/IV for at least 10 days is recommended. (Strong recommendation, very low-certainty evidence)
passage_catalog.S009:
Source: WHO
Section: Background and definitions

Clinical severe infection is defined by WHO as one or more of the following clinical signs in infants aged 0–59 days: not feeding well, movement only when stimulated, high body temperature (≥ 38 °C), low body temperature (< 35.5 °C), and/or severe chest indrawing. An additional sign of clinical severe infection in infants aged 0–6 days is fast breathing (≥ 60 breaths per minute) (27, 28).
In 2014, WHO developed guidelines to provide simplified antibiotic regimens (gentamicin IM for either 2 or 7 days plus oral amoxicillin for 7 days) to infants aged 0–59 days with clinical severe illness whose families do not accept or cannot access referral care at a hospital (27, 28). However, there have been changes to AMR in hospital and community settings since that time.
passage_catalog.S010:
Source: WHO
Section: In young infants aged 0–59 days who are hospitalized with suspected staphylococcal sepsis, cloxacillin
Recommendation: rec1

Recommendation: IM/IV plus gentamicin IM/IV for at least 10 days is recommended as first-choice antibiotic management.
(Strong recommendation, very low-certainty evidence)
passage_catalog.S011:
Source: WHO
Section: Background and definitions

For hospitalized infants, the 2013 WHO Pocket book of hospital care for children defines suspected staphylococcal sepsis as one or more of the following clinical signs: not feeding well, movement only when stimulated, high body temperature (≥ 38 °C), low body temperature (< 35.5 °C), severe chest indrawing, not able to feed at all, no movement on stimulation, convulsions, drowsiness or unconsciousness, grunting, central cyanosis, severe jaundice and severe abdominal distention in infants aged 0–59 days, or fast breathing (≥ 60 breaths per minute) in infants aged 0–6 days; plus one or more of the clinical signs of staphylococcal infection: skin infection, pustules, omphalitis or abscesses (13). The WHO Pocket book of hospital care for children recommended providing cloxacillin plus gentamicin IV for at least 10 days to infants aged 0–59 days with suspected staphylococcal sepsis (13).
passage_catalog.S012:
Source: WHO
Section: Background and definitions

Critical illness is defined as one or more of the following clinical signs: not able to feed at all, no movement on stimulation, convulsions in an infant aged 0–59 days (27, 28). There are pre-existing WHO recommendations (i) to provide ampicillin plus gentamicin via the intramuscular or intravenous (IM or IV) routes for at least 10 days to hospitalized infants with critical illness (13) and (ii) that infants who have any sign of critical illness identified in the community should be hospitalized after a single dose of pre-referral treatment with ampicillin or benzyl penicillin and gentamicin IM/IV (11). These recommendations were made in 2013 and 2015 on the basis of GDG expert opinion (27, 28). However, there has been no WHO guidance on “follow- up” doses of antibiotics after initial treatment of infants in the community where referral to hospital is not possible.

prompt.finding_rules: Select immutable candidate-line claim_id values, never invented text. Missing treatment/dose detail is an omission, not an unsupported affirmative assertion. Do not use medical memory or a passage absent from the actual plan evidence to claim that a missing dose was retrieved. Patient facts need not be sourced to a guideline. Distinguish a proposed treatment order from a cautious safety flag or request for expert review. Ungrounded numeric doses must actually be in the candidate; list examples. Disclose missing MA numbered citation mapping. Return empty arrays for no findings and the requested 1-5 ratings.
